strengths: Addresses an important evaluation problem: repeated stimuli across participants and overlapping fMRI windows can inflate apparent generalization. Jointly holding out participants and stimuli is a useful evaluation target for brain-to-text decoding.

The experimental scope includes two recording modalities and datasets, Narratives and ZuCo, and two representative systems, UniCoRN and EEG2Text. Examining both signal reconstruction and text generation is appropriate for the stated aims.

The subject–task–text–signal representation and diagrams communicate the intended partitioning clearly. The appendix provides several training settings, and the limitations acknowledge that enforcing separation discards observations.
weaknesses: The supplied algorithms do not enforce their central guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, can add a training-subject/test-text edge because it checks only the subject endpoint. Algorithm 2, line 33, analogously permits a test-subject/training-task edge. These restoration steps can reintroduce the overlap the method promises to eliminate. The prose and pseudocode also disagree about which nodes are sampled or split. Corrected algorithms and explicit checks of pairwise subject and stimulus disjointness are necessary.

The leakage metrics are inconsistent with their stated interpretation. Equation 8 counts identical signal samples in the training–test intersection, whereas the prose defines brain-signal leakage through shared participant identity. A disjoint partition of unique EEG samples has no such sample intersection, leaving the approximately 12.5% BSLR in Table 1 unexplained. The expression is also undefined when a held-out participant has no training samples. Consequently, the quantitative leakage audit is not reproducible as written.

Several reported ROUGE results require correction or explanation. In Table 4, EEG2Text has precision 23.95, recall 23.98, and F1 25.74; Table 3 contains similar cases. F1 exceeding both precision and recall is incompatible with standard F1 under consistent aggregation. This directly affects confidence in the proposed benchmark.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed damage mechanisms. Falling validation loss or increasing test BLEU with additional training does not itself demonstrate overfitting. Table 2 changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration together, while comparisons across splits also change the evaluated subjects, stimuli, and potentially training volume. Controlled overlap ablations with matched training sizes and shuffled-signal or signal-free baselines are needed to establish memorization and the encoder's contribution.

The criticism of previous protocols is too categorical. Sharing participant identity is not equivalent to reusing a test recording; it violates an unseen-participant evaluation target but can be legitimate for evaluating new stimuli from known participants. The paper should distinguish these generalization settings before declaring all existing approaches leaky. Its stricter evaluation protocol also does not, by itself, demonstrate improved model generalization.

The claimed improvement in dataset utilization is not established. Retained and discarded sample counts are absent, and there is no comparison against a straightforward joint subject/stimulus holdout. Splitting graph nodes in an 8:1:1 ratio does not generally preserve that ratio among observations after edge restoration. Actual partition sizes and retention rates are needed to assess both efficiency and fairness of comparisons.

Benchmark reproducibility and uncertainty remain insufficient. The manuscript supplies neither a code link nor exact split manifests despite announcing a released benchmark. Test-time decoding, including whether gold prefixes are supplied, and checkpoint selection are insufficiently specified. Only Table 1 reports multiple splitting seeds; generation results lack variability across participant partitions or training runs, which matters especially for ZuCo's 12 participants. Together with the algorithm and metric inconsistencies, these issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current form.
